issues.author: rjpower
issues.body:
## Background

Finelog is our ingestion and query service for logs, metrics and telemetry. Nearly all of our logging data is sent to finelog for stable storage. Each cluster runs a finelog server for tasks running on that cluster; per-cluster data is forwarded to the shared finelog *hub*, which also serves queries for Iris (log fetching, RPC stats, host memory usage, etc.) and Grafana.

Finelog has grown organically, which has exposed a few design problems:

- Finelog writes to local SSD first, then archives to GCS. Once objects age out of local storage they are no longer queryable via the finelog server and must be queried manually.
- Finelog does not strongly separate telemetry (periodically sampled, strongly typed data, e.g. from training runs) from logs (unstructured, time-ordered log lines).
- Indexing, partitioning and query optimization are ad-hoc.

Together these produce occasionally slow or hard-to-optimize queries, and unnecessary load on the finelog server that could be offloaded to clients. Maintaining and hand-optimizing this takes time away from more productive work.

## Proposal

Move Finelog to be "object store first": write records and compact directly to the object store, and use the transition as an opportunity to fix partitioning and indexing.

The finelog server remains the primary ingestion path and the query path for ad-hoc queries, but the new model adds *client directed queries*: clients can request the *catalog* from the finelog server (all segments, their indices, and the partitioning scheme) and use it to issue direct reads against stored segments. This removes finelog as a scaling bottleneck for queries and as a source of failure.

## Success criteria

- No longer stages to local disk (we may optionally stage L0 shards if going straight to the object store is a problem).
- A comprehensive schema policy framework for describing a *schema* (a typed set of records):
  - how data in the schema is partitioned (hive partitioning by date, etc.)
  - what indices to construct
  - sort & grouping order for segments
- The Finelog client supports both `server` and `client` based query models, with the client resolving directly against GCS objects.
- A reusable migration model for online updates of existing schemas without downtime — e.g. changing hive partitioning to introduce year/month/date bucketing.
- Performance comparable to the current setup for our Grafana dashboards.

## Approach

Mostly extending and improving existing features. New pieces:

**Per-schema policy registration.** A clean mechanism to describe ingestion, compaction, partitioning and indexing plans for a schema. For example, levanter metrics might be hive-partitioned by month and day, sorted by `{run-id, feature, seq-id}`, and indexed on run-id. This enables efficient "what are all of the run-ids" queries, a natural query retirement policy (drop older dates), and efficient lookup of per-feature series.

**Online migration.** Extending a schema is "free" today (adding columns doesn't perturb existing segments), but removing indices or changing partitioning is not and currently requires careful manual migration. Borrowing from Postgres, we'll use a primitive MVCC mechanism: versioning plus dual writes make migration safe and incremental. A schema or partition break triggers a new Finelog version; multiple versions can be active for ingestion but only one is active for querying at a time. Once bulk older segments are migrated, the query version is flipped and the older version can be deleted.

**Cleaning up objects.** Making GCS canonical means we also need to clean it up: existing GCS artifacts are archival only and don't necessarily follow the same indexing or clustering policies as live objects. We propose a one-time archival of these old objects for safe-keeping, as they are rarely/never queried today. Going forward all objects are kept in a maintained state, and since the object store is globally accessible we can use e.g. Iris jobs for bulk maintenance events.

## Rollout

We want to do this migration once, so we'll test locally and on `marin-dev` before final deployment. Many of the required features already exist: if we only wanted to offload to object storage, we could likely do so simply by changing our output disk targets and measuring the performance effect.

## Expected timeframe

~1 week of work, overlappable with other ongoing projects. Most of the work is in validation and rollout.

## Alternatives considered

- **Do nothing**, and just bump disk size and schema size limits to allow deeper queries. Rejected as a long-term fix: it results in increasingly expensive queries and periodic manual maintenance events to bump disk volume size.
- **Adopt an alternative ingestion engine**, e.g. [Lance](https://lancedb.github.io/lance/) or [Iceberg](https://iceberg.apache.org/), both of which appear to be mature log/metric service engines. Since fixing Finelog to have effectively unbounded capacity looks like a relatively small amount of work, and it supports the exact tuning and patterns we use, we defer adoption of these for later.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Assessment:** design proposal, not a bug fix. This spans the Rust store, policy/migration framework, the Python client, and deploy/archival, and the author scopes it at ~1 week. Per the fix-issue workflow I'm not opening a PR; below is a current-state map plus a proposed decomposition for review. The main finding: most of the required machinery already exists, so this is largely extension + a rollout, not greenfield.

**Current state vs. the five success criteria**

- *No local-disk staging.* Today the store is local-first with a `LOCAL -> BOTH -> REMOTE` sync surface to `gs://`/`s3://` (`lib/finelog/rust/src/store/remote.rs`, `store/reconcile.rs`, `store/store.rs`). "Object-store first" means either writing L1+ straight to remote or keeping only an L0 stage — the criterion's own escape hatch. This is the largest behavioral change and where the Grafana-parity risk lives.
- *Per-schema policy framework.* Programmable per-namespace storage and physical partitioning already exist: `rust/src/storage_policy.rs`, `rust/src/partition_policy.rs` (versioned `SegmentPartition { spec_id, values }`, hive-style, additive), plus `ingestion_policy.rs`, `levanter_metrics_policy.rs`, `telemetry_policy.rs`. Secondary indices (trigram/exact/value-counts/covering projections) are described in `lib/finelog/AGENTS.md` under "Secondary indexes." The gap is a single clean *registration* entry point, not the primitives.
- *Client-directed queries.* Missing today. The Python `LogClient` is server-only (`lib/finelog/src/finelog/client/log_client.py`); there is no catalog-fetch + direct-GCS-read path. This is the one genuinely new subsystem: a `GetCatalog`-style RPC exposing segments/indices/partition spec, plus a client planner that resolves against object-store segments.
- *Online migration (MVCC).* A migration framework exists (`rust/src/migrations/mod.rs`, `migrations/telemetry_v1.rs`, `bin/finelog-migrate.rs`) and `spec_id` already makes layout changes additive/queryable across versions. The proposal's versioning + dual-write + query-version flip extends this to partition/index breaks; check whether the current single-`spec_id` model needs an explicit active-ingest-vs-active-query version pointer in the catalog (`rust/src/store/catalog.rs`, which already persists `forward_state`).
- *Legacy GCS cleanup.* One-time archival of pre-policy objects; no maintained-state guarantee for archived data today. Lowest-risk piece, doable as an Iris bulk job as the issue suggests.

**Proposed decomposition (each a reviewable PR, roughly in dependency order)**

1. Policy registration API — consolidate the existing storage/partition/index policies behind one per-schema registration surface; no behavior change, unblocks the rest.
2. Object-store-first writer — remote-canonical L1+ (optional L0 stage) behind a policy flag; validate on `marin-dev` with `telemetry_layout_bench` / `grafana_dashboard_bench` before flipping any prod namespace.
3. Catalog RPC + client-directed reads — new `GetCatalog` and a client that reads segments directly; server query path stays the default.
4. Migration versioning — active-ingest vs active-query version with dual writes and a flip, layered on the existing `spec_id`/migration framework.
5. Legacy archival + maintenance — one-time archival and going-forward GCS hygiene.

Open questions for a human before implementation: (a) L0 staging — keep a local L0 or go fully remote for ingest? (b) does client-directed query need its own authz path, given the server's default-deny auth gate is what protects reads today? (c) catalog freshness/consistency contract for direct client reads against a mutating store.

Refs: `lib/finelog/AGENTS.md` (schema-ownership, indexing, forwarding), `lib/finelog/OPS.md`, and the prior layout work in `.agents/projects/finelog_telemetry_layout/`. Recommend converting the accepted decomposition into tracked sub-issues before coding.

🤖 Research

Finelog currently acknowledges writes after local Parquet and SQLite persistence; [remote sync](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/a9a070c2211e920549ea6e168076b2116b1d7d4f/lib/finelog/rust/src/store/remote.rs#L124) archives L1+ Parquet, while [query planning](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/a9a070c2211e920549ea6e168076b2116b1d7d4f/lib/finelog/rust/src/query/provider.rs#L103) registers only local files. The repository already has physical [policy primitives](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/a9a070c2211e920549ea6e168076b2116b1d7d4f/lib/finelog/rust/src/policies.rs#L22) and a resumable [migration precedent](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/a9a070c2211e920549ea6e168076b2116b1d7d4f/lib/finelog/rust/src/migrations/telemetry_v1.rs#L36), but no remotely recoverable catalog, remote query visibility, or versioned table specification. The duplicate-work preflight found no open implementation PR for #8737.

Proposed Fix

Add a dormant object-native path that flushes the existing bounded Arrow buffer to immutable segment objects, publishes one complete namespace catalog per generation, and selects it by conditional `HEAD` update; SQLite and local files become recoverable projections of that catalog. Use one object-aware DataFusion path for server and direct-client execution, with client-side catalog reads, best-effort query reporting, and maximum-query-time MVCC garbage collection. Accept only monotonic `TableSpec` updates and let Finelog automatically dual-write, backfill, verify, and activate them; validate first with `file://` fault tests and disposable copied stores before any marin-dev enablement.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 Research

The hub has no version-0 tables, but the three regional forwarders still recover legacy-local catalogs from their object archives after each node-local Pod replacement. The forward cursor advances only after the hub accepts a batch, while object maintenance currently collects only objects made unreachable by another catalog mutation; it does not retire live segments at the cursor. The existing legacy eviction path preserves LOCAL-only segments, and version-0 migration excludes REMOTE archive rows, so the transition can shrink each forwarder to its unarchived tail before rewriting.

Relevant paths: [forwarding cursor](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/61e59be455662c5d0cfec042417abe50f2b5ed00/lib/finelog/rust/src/server/forwarding.rs), [legacy eviction](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/61e59be455662c5d0cfec042417abe50f2b5ed00/lib/finelog/rust/src/store/legacy/archive.rs), [migration source selection](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/61e59be455662c5d0cfec042417abe50f2b5ed00/lib/finelog/rust/src/store/table/spec_migration.rs), and [object maintenance](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/61e59be455662c5d0cfec042417abe50f2b5ed00/lib/finelog/rust/src/store/table/maintenance.rs).

Proposed Fix

Add a relay maintenance profile for deployments with a forwarding target. It will skip derived-artifact and terminal-layout work, retire whole object segments only after their maximum sequence is covered by the durable forwarding cursor, and preserve bytes through the existing state and orphan grace windows. Add a drain/status gate, migrate the forwarders after legacy eviction leaves only LOCAL-only tails, then remove the version-0 runtime after the fleet reports no legacy tables.

This tracker keeps the dense Qwen3-8B TPU inference parity matrix readable and current for Levanter versus vLLM-TPU. Current anchors show Levanter close on v6e decode-heavy (`0.938` decode tok/s ratio), below target on v6e mixed (`0.819`), still below target on v6e prefill-heavy after corrected and post-split reruns (`0.742` to `0.758`), and substantially behind on the bounded v5p TP=4 mixed row (`0.600`). ### Helpful links
- Parent rollout epic: #6227
- Dense matrix harness PR: #6176
- Admission/timing fields PR: #6185
- Prefill-heavy follow-up: #6229
- v5p follow-up: #6230

## Description
Finish and maintain the dense Qwen3-8B TPU inference parity matrix for Levanter versus vLLM-TPU. Report results by regime instead of collapsing them into one average: greedy `n=1`, sampled `n=4`, `o128`, `o512`, likely `o2048`, logprobs on/off, decode-heavy, mixed, prefill-heavy, pressure, and churn cases.

PR #6176 (`codex/qwen3-dense-parity-matrix`, head `104bf901e33c5f0b34d32d4f59edf27b82f66714`) carries the dense matrix harness/config and has all visible checks green. PR #6185 head `f55913d1a9770b7ebdfb051150972e649644526e` adds the current admission/timing fields needed for the next rows, including the prefill-drain versus generation-loop split.

Current runtime anchors:
- v6e decode-heavy `decode_b32_i1_o128_n4`: `3197.58` Levanter vs `3408.09` vLLM decode tok/s, ratio `0.938`.
- v6e mixed `mixed_b32_i512_o512_n1`: `4084.24` Levanter vs `4985.21` vLLM decode tok/s, ratio `0.819`, all `16384` expected completion tokens.

- [x] Matrix rows are reproducible from committed benchmark config.

issues.author: WhenWen
issues.body:
🤖 Tracking issue for adding the KL SOAP H optimizer to the grug-moe pipeline.

## Variant

Reproduce the `KLSOAPH` optimizer from [KellerJordan/modded-nanogpt PR #290](https://github.com/KellerJordan/modded-nanogpt/pull/290) inside marin grug-moe. 

The implementation is a fresh JAX/optax port of upstream `KLSOAPH.step()`: per-leaf SOAP state (`exp_avg`, `exp_avg_sq`, `gg_l`, `gg_r`, `q_l`, `q_r`), `eigh` refresh every `precond_freq` steps via `lax.cond`, Adam in the eigenbasis, project back. Wraps `_scale_invariant_hyperball_updates` for the post-step. Three-group routing mirrors `GrugMoeMuonHConfig`: `klsoaph` for matrices, `adamh` for `lm_head`/`output_proj`, `adam` for the baseline-Adam group.

## Deviations from upstream

- `precond_freq = 5` (upstream default 1). Eigendecomposition is the dominant per-step cost; refreshing every 5 steps keeps the eigenbasis fresh while amortizing the eigh.
- The attention gate parameter (`attn_gate`) is routed to the SOAP matrix group instead of plain Adam (variant-only override via a new `_uses_klsoaph_baseline_adam_group` predicate; MuonH/NorMuonH unchanged).

## Gate plan

Follow `experiments/grug/moe/agent.md`:

- **Gate 1**: d512 (2.19e17 FLOPs), d768 (1.70e18 FLOPs). Pass criterion: effective speedup > 1× vs canonical baseline at *both* scales.
- **Gate 2**: add d1024 (9.00e18 FLOPs), d1280 (2.83e19 FLOPs). Pass criterion: speedup at all four scales, and 4-point pinned-`L_inf=1.6` scaling-law fit projects under the canonical baseline at both 1e21 (2.606) and 1e23 (2.252).

Baseline scaling law (canonical, from `experiments/grug/moe/agent.md`):

```
L(C) = 1.6 + 95.18 · C^(-0.0941)
```

## PR

- Implementation + sweep script + tests: filed as a PR against the parent research branch (linked once opened).

## Status checklist

- [x] `scale_by_klsoaph` JAX transform implemented (`experiments/grug/moe/klsoaph.py`)
- [x] `GrugMoeKLSoapHConfig` added (`experiments/grug/moe/optimizer.py`)
- [x] Variant override: `attn_gate` to klsoaph (`_uses_klsoaph_baseline_adam_group`)
- [x] `experiments/grug/moe/klsoaph_sweep.py` with `KLSOAPH_GATE` env var
- [x] Unit tests (mask routing, state geometry, single-device update, sharded-mesh, sweep wiring)
- [x] Sharding-ambiguity fix on the `model` axis (replicate state + explicit `out_sharding`)
- [ ] Gate-1 run (d512, d768) on us-east5 preemptible
- [ ] Gate-1 verdict (loss, speedup vs baseline)
- [ ] Gate-2 run (d1024, d1280)
- [ ] 4-point scaling-law fit + projection at 1e21 / 1e23
- [ ] Final verdict

comments.author: WhenWen
comments.body:
🤖 **Gate-1 verdict: FAIL — KL Soap H underperforms the AdamH baseline at both scales.**

## Final metrics

| Scale | C (FLOPs) | KL Soap H | AdamH baseline | Δ vs baseline | Speedup |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **d512** | 2.19e17 | paloma macro **4.145** (uncheat 4.077, micro 3.925) | 3.8104 | +0.335 worse | **0.24×** |
| **d768** | 1.70e18 | paloma macro **3.698** (uncheat 3.495, micro 3.462) | 3.4339 | +0.264 worse | **0.24×** |

Speedup computed against the canonical AdamH scaling law `L(C) = 1.6 + 95.18·C^(-0.0941)` from `experiments/grug/moe/agent.md:30` (i.e., at the same final loss, AdamH would need ~0.24× the compute KL Soap H used).

For reference, MuonH no-warmup (issue #5619) was 1.49× / 1.34× vs baseline at the same scales. So this isn't an infrastructure issue — the existing matrix-preconditioner pipeline works; KL Soap H specifically is the underperformer.

**Not proceeding to gate 2** — agent.md requires effective speedup ≥ 1× at both gate-1 scales.

## Diagnostics

Likely contributors (any of these could be the dominant one):

1. **Hyperparameters from upstream may not transfer.** Upstream uses `lr=0.018, beta1=0.9, beta2=0.9, shampoo_beta=0.9` on modded-nanogpt's GPT-2 small at fixed budget. The grug-moe pipeline supplies `learning_rate` from the heuristic and `beta1/beta2` defaults differ from MuonH (`beta2=0.9` vs `beta2=0.95` for MuonH/AdamH). I didn't sweep these.
2. **`precond_freq=5` may be too sparse for these small scales.** Upstream uses `precond_freq=1`; user direction was to amortize at 5. At d512 with ~6.4k steps, that means only ~1.3k eigenbasis refreshes — possibly too few when GG matrices are still moving fast in the early-/mid-warmup regime (here, there is no warmup at all).
3. **`attn_gate` routing to klsoaph may be destabilizing.** The variant moves a small `(hidden_dim, num_heads)` parameter out of plain Adam into the SOAP matrix group. SOAP's eigenbasis projection on a heavily-sharded thin matrix may degenerate; nothing in the code or tests would catch a numerical-quality regression there.
4. **JAX/optax port may have a subtle math bug** vs upstream PyTorch. I deferred the PyTorch-equivalence test (`tests/test_klsoaph_against_pytorch.py`) — the in-pipeline tests only verify wiring, not numerical match. The most likely suspect spots: eigenbasis sign-flipping (upstream doesn't fix sign, I don't either, but XLA's eigh sort order may differ); the Adam-in-eigenbasis bias correction (upstream does no bias correction, I match that); the GG-EMA division by cols/rows (matches upstream).

The gap is too large for a narrow tuning miss — likely either (3) the attn_gate inclusion or (4) a math/dtype regression. Worth investigating separately if there's interest, but the gate-1 result kills the current variant as-is.

## Status

- d512 SUCCEEDED in parent `/kaiyue/iris-run-job-20260514-015907` at 11:29 UTC May 14 (~9h after launch).
- d768 SUCCEEDED in parent `/kaiyue/iris-run-job-20260515-073917` at 09:44 UTC May 16 (after one mid-run resubmit because the previous parent task stayed pending re-allocation for ~2 babysit cycles, picked up via the saved abandoned-child rule).
- Babysitter cron `1e2dedf0` deleted.
- PR #5729 still open — the optimizer + sweep code itself works (tests pass, sharding handled, training completes); just the variant doesn't beat the baseline. Closing thoughts depend on whether you want to keep the code merged for future iterations or close out the PR.

**Pollution bug (fixed).** A prior "subspace_frac" refactor had rewritten the default eigenbasis refresh `qr(GG@q)` as `q@qr(qᵀGGq)`. Algebraically equal for orthogonal `q`, but forming `P=qᵀGGq` **squares** the (already ill-conditioned) gradient-Gram condition number — the eigenbasis degrades over a long run (orthonormality error grew ~180× over 800 steps in a numerical test). Every run launched after that commit stalled at train-loss ~6.0 (including *linear*-schedule runs, ruling out the LR schedule); runs before it trained cleanly to ~3.2. Reverted to the exact `qr(GG@q)` — optimizer core now byte-identical to pre-pollution. Stopped all polluted in-flight runs.

**Understanding the ~24-min compile (new <10-min criterion).** Per-step linalg = `qr×2` (refresh) + `eigh×2` (init branch — compiled even though it only runs at step 1). Isolated compiles are small (eigh 13s, qr ≤10s), so the 24 min is the full graph. Identified a likely **double-compile**: `opt.init` produces *replicated* state but the sharded step returns `mat_p`, so step-1 and step-2+ have different input shardings → two full compiles.

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
WHAT WE DID

Ran a sweep over four agentic data sources across a variety of hyperparameter configurations: Calendar instruction-following v3, Calendar agent v2, BugsInPy v4, and SWE-Gym v5

WHY WE DID IT

In order to establish a strong baseline set of configurations and datasets for future experiments in agentic RL

RESULTS

* This is the first experiment to establish decisive RL reward advantage in agentic SWE tasks on certain sources; pass@1 after RL was generally comparable to pass@16 before RL on the val set
* Holdout val set improvement is the most reliable way to evaluate the progress of the policy; reward trends across a run are noisy and don't reliably show improvement, and the question of task source relevance to downstream eval performance should be treated as a separate consideration and optimized independently
* The optimal loss reduction strategy appears to vary considerably by task source, as does the number of rollout engines required; this is to be expected because both properties condition, to an extent, on the verbosity of the selected policy
* Group size appears to operate as a kind of regularization (perhaps confounded here by reduced relative batch size in arms with larger group size) -- at larger group sizes, the model is less likely to make rapid, dramatic improvements on the val set. Entropy collapse remains a significant risk in larger groups
* SWE-flavored sources with diverse codebases are generally slower than simpler agentic tool-use codebases, because rollouts are longer and involve more tool calls. There is also a high degree of variance within SWE-flavored sources w.r.t. overall step time
* In the near-sync regime, the dominant step-time slowdown comes from slow verifiers and slow environment execution of agent actions (both of which point to slow execution within containers, but fast communication between Harbor and the containers)
* In the async regime, slow verifiers and slow environment execution persist but are masked by the larger mass of rollouts generated; however, this can introduce off-policy learning pathology at higher async step counts (>=2) and should be avoided where possible
* SWE-Gym showed slow, modest improvement under RL but the 30-turn cap was excessively limiting; for datasets like SWE-Gym, agent timeout and turn cap limit will probably need to be set quite high to allow the model to learn a useful policy, at least initially
* Group size 8 was a clear winner on BugsinPy; however, the group size 4 run was terminated prematurely by the agent and the larger group sizes may have been handicapped primarily by the proportionately smaller batch sizes. We leave a complete, principled group-size / batch-size / runtime trade-off to future work

issues.author: mcwitt
issues.body:
Two GB200 NVL72 domains on `cw-us-east-08a` show fabric-level faults that have now cost the production hero a restart and are the leading explanation for the ragged-EP hangs in #8870. Filing separately because the asks are infrastructure-side and independent of any Marin code.

## 1. `dh1-r137` (rack index 10 in every hero placement): contained NVLink fault took down the hero

2026-09-05 17:19:31Z: `hero-wd-gate-router-p02-step58k` completed step 65069 and then stalled silently for fifteen minutes with every rank blocked on the device. At 17:34:36.549Z task 162 rank 1 on **`s2grxs64`** logged `CUDA_ERROR_CONTAINED: Invalid access of peer GPU memory over nvlink or a hardware error` (`gpu_cudamallocasync_allocator.cc:414`); the seven other nodes of the domain followed within 0.5 s (`s5k62nb4`, `s24qxs64`, `s91qxs64`, `s1zsxs64`, `s3ztxs64`, `s92vxs64`, …), and every rack within 7 s via fate sharing. The gang restarted from the hourly checkpoint; cost 125 steps plus 20 minutes. GPU-side NVLink error counters on the domain's 64 GPUs did not move across the event (read-only `nvidia-smi nvlink -e` before and after), so the fault is switch-side or a non-link hardware error. `dmesg`/XIDs are not visible from the task containers.

## 2. `dh1-r129` (rack index 8): a flapping NVLink and a 10× slow multicast bind

- **`s9jvxs64` GPU 0, link 14: 505 link recovery events lifetime, +3 in a 21-minute sample (01:53-02:13Z) and +1 more by 21:30Z**, while the production hero ran on it. Across three read-only sweeps of 320 GPUs × 18 links on five racks it is the only NVLink error counter that moved at all; every symbol/Rx/discard counter on every link is zero.
- At the start of the 2026-09-04 eleven-rack window, this domain's first NVLS multicast bind (`symTeamObtain`, between `NVLS Created Multicast group nranks 64` and the first `cuMulticastBindAddr`) took **5.50 s against 0.44-0.63 s on the other ten racks**, uniform to ±8 ms across all 64 GPUs — an excess of 5.009 s, a round five seconds, i.e. a timeout-then-succeed in a fabric-side path. One-shot; the second bind was normal.
- This is the exact node set (`s38vxs64 … shmsxs64`) on which the ragged hero stalled in #8870 attempt 0 on 2026-09-02.

## 3. What the training-side telemetry adds

The 2026-09-04 window's per-launch barrier-wait marks (see #8870) show one GPU per rack arriving 25-160 ms late at a random layer's all-to-all, ≥11× more often on rack indices 8, 9 and 10 (`dh1-r129`, `r136`, `r137`) than on the other eight, with nothing upstream of the GPU to blame (communicators, host, data loader and step-entry skew all measured flat). A link retrain stalls whatever is crossing the link for tens to hundreds of milliseconds, which is that shape.

## Asks

1. Node-level `dmesg`/XID history and fabric-manager / NVSwitch logs for `dh1-r137` around 2026-09-05 17:19-17:35Z and for `dh1-r129` around 2026-09-04 22:35:04-09Z.
2. Diagnosis of `s9jvxs64` GPU 0 link 14 (and its switch port); it is still recovering under load.
3. A per-rack NVLink health signal Iris can read before placing a gang (recovery-event rate, or a first-bind timing probe), so a known-bad domain is not handed to a 704-GPU hero. Placement is deterministic here — these domains have held rack indices 8-10 in every hero and window placement since 09-02 — so the same hardware keeps landing under the same job.

Related: #8870 (the ragged hang this most likely explains), #8925 (Kueue gate that prevents choosing racks), #8912 (Iris does not record accelerator telemetry).

stack (#8063), and the GPU wheel now discovers its `_C` extension by shape across the
CUDA 13 / stable-ABI boundary (#8250). This issue tracks the work that remains after

   explicit no-op summary either way.

   `vllm` and `tpu-inference` forks; a Marin-controlled index would let serve, eval,

6. Resolve the Marin-owned pin audit (#6480). Decide whether Levanter can move to a

Building the [eval FineStore explorer](https://applets.marina.oa.dev/a/8fb60a25-7a53-44a5-9fda-5540c1580695/) exposed gaps between package validation and the deployed applet environment. `marina publish --dry-run` accepted a package whose backend later failed with `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'evaldash'`. After bundling the reader, Chromium rejected the frontend's inline script under Marina's `script-src 'self'` policy. A local Python import also created `server/__pycache__/*.pyc`, which made the next package build fail.

Improve the applet development loop so these constraints are visible before publication and existing functionality can be reused without copying app modules.

Done when:

- A local validation command can check backend imports using the applet runtime's module path and reports which checks it performed. Package-only validation explicitly identifies what it has not checked.
- Validation detects inline scripts that conflict with Marina's content security policy, or offers a browser smoke check that reports the violation. The starter package demonstrates compliant external scripts.

- Documentation defines how applets can reuse Python helpers from checked-in Marina apps or shared installed packages, with a supported example for sharing eval sample readers without copying the reader into the applet.

- An object-store browser example demonstrates shallow directory expansion, a request deadline, and a listing cache in the applet's Postgres schema.

The initial recursive object-store scan was an applet implementation mistake: it issued hundreds of sequential listings in one request. issues.author: dlwh
issues.body:
Allow Grug MoE backends to exclude padded positions from expert dispatch, capacity accounting, and expert computation. Carry token validity from the model's attention mask into the MoE path; a padding token ID alone is not sufficient because the same ID can appear at a valid position.

In the Snowball 67B RL trial on 32 H100s (PP4/EP8, ragged all-to-all, capacity factor 2), the first microbatch contained 42,435 padded positions out of 68,160 (62.26%). Routing rejected 1,559,713 of 7,088,640 assignments across 26 layers, and the no-drop guard stopped the run before an optimizer update. Padding contributes to capacity demand; the fraction of rejected assignments belonging to valid tokens has not been measured. The ragged backend reports these as sender drops, although clipping is applied to receiver expert-chunk capacity.

Packing is being added separately. For the complete 512-trajectory capture, Levanter's packing reduces overall padding from 55.10% to 15.49% after alignment to eight GPUs, so residual padding still needs handling.

Done when:

- Invalid positions consume no expert capacity and produce no dispatched expert rows or expert-parameter gradient contributions.
- When valid assignments fit capacity, valid-token outputs, loss, and gradients match an equivalent unpadded, dropless computation within existing numerical tolerances. Adding padding does not change which valid assignments are accepted, including when valid demand exceeds capacity.
- Tests cover mixed sequence lengths, packed segment boundaries, all-padding local shards, and distributed forward/backward execution without collective mismatches.
- Routing metrics distinguish valid assignments, skipped padding, and genuine capacity drops. A padded workload benchmark reports the memory and runtime effect.

Start with `moe_mlp` in `lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/grug_moe.py` and the ragged backend in `lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_ragged_all_to_all.py`.

Evidence: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/users/dlwh/skyrl/migration/june-ragged-67b-benchmark-20260907-02/drops.json`, `capture-padding.json` under the same prefix, and `s3://marin-us-east-02a/users/dlwh/skyrl/migration/june-packing-census-20260907-01/census.json`.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:**
- [x] Read fix-issue and commit skills, AGENTS.md
- [x] Investigate Grug MoE dispatch/capacity path and how token validity flows
- [x] Assess scope — feature-scale (multi-backend + metrics + distributed tests + benchmark), no PR
- [x] Post root-cause analysis and proposed approach

## Research

The MoE path has no concept of token validity. `moe_mlp` and every EP backend accept only `x [T,D]`, `selected_experts [T,K]`, and `combine_weights [T,K]`; padded positions are ordinary rows and route like any token ([`grug_moe.py` L146-161](lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/grug_moe.py#L146-L161)). In the ragged backend, demand is `group_sizes = bincount(flat_selected, length=num_experts)` and capacity is `ceil(capacity_factor * tokens_per_shard * topk)`, so padded assignments count as real demand, get clipped against capacity, are dispatched and run through the expert MLP, and contribute expert-parameter gradients ([`ep_ragged_all_to_all.py` L328-345](lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_ragged_all_to_all.py#L328-L345)). The reported drops are then `sum(group_sizes) - accepted_local`, which conflates padding with genuine capacity drops of valid tokens ([L420-422](lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/ep_ragged_all_to_all.py#L420-L422)) — consistent with the 62% padding and 22% rejected-assignments observation and the no-drop guard tripping. As the issue notes, a padding token id cannot identify padding (the same id can appear at a valid position), so validity must come from the attention mask / segment ids.

## Proposed approach (for review before implementation)

Thread an optional validity mask and make invalid positions consume no capacity, no dispatched rows, and no expert-parameter gradients, while keeping all buffer shapes statically sized on the worst case so no collective shapes change.

1. **API.** Add `token_valid: Bool[Array, "T"] | None = None` to `MoEExpertMlp.__call__` → `moe_mlp` → each `_moe_mlp_ep_*_local` and `_moe_mlp_local`. `None` means all-valid, preserving current behavior and existing tests. Derive the mask in the model from the attention mask / segment ids (grug attention already exposes `segment_ids` metadata via `thd_segment_metadata_from_segment_ids`).
2. **Ragged backend.** Before `bincount`, remap invalid tokens' `flat_selected` to a sentinel expert (`num_experts`) so `bincount(length=num_experts)` drops them from `group_sizes`. Their sorted assignments land past every real group, so `_expert_granular_a2a_params` never sends them — no receiver capacity, no dispatched rows, no expert-param grads. `[TK]`/`[C]` buffers stay static; only the counts feeding `group_sizes`/clipping change. Zero invalid tokens' `combine_weights` as belt-and-suspenders (the unpermute already reads unwritten slots as zero).
3. **Other backends.** Apply the equivalent capacity-accounting exclusion to `ep_fixed_all_to_all`, `ep_fixed_pooled_wave_all_to_all`, `ep_ring`, `ep_deepep`, and `local` — each computes capacity/clipping differently.
4. **Metrics.** Extend `CapacityOverflow` (or the routing metrics) to distinguish valid assignments dispatched, skipped-padding assignments, and genuine capacity drops of valid tokens, replacing the padding-conflated `dropped_local`.
5. **Invariants to preserve** (from Done-when): with `token_valid=None` outputs are bit-identical to today; when valid demand fits capacity, valid outputs/loss/grads match an unpadded dropless reference within existing tolerances; adding padding never changes which valid assignments are accepted (the sentinel keeps valid group prefixes and clip decisions independent of padding).
6. **Tests / benchmark.** Mixed sequence lengths, packed segment boundaries, an all-padding local shard (zero output, no collective mismatch), and distributed forward/backward equivalence vs. an unpadded reference; plus a padded-workload benchmark reporting memory and runtime.

Files: `grug_moe.py`, `_moe/{ep_ragged_all_to_all,ep_fixed_all_to_all,ep_fixed_pooled_wave_all_to_all,ep_ring,ep_deepep,local,common}.py`, and the training MoE MLP block that threads the mask. Scope spans multiple backends and distributed tests, so this is larger than a self-contained fix; handing it to a human to confirm the sentinel-remap design and metric shape before implementation.

## TL;DR

Gate 1 failed. Learned norm-preserving residual mixing reached `1.018x` effective speedup at d512 but `0.950x` at d768; both widths had to exceed `1.0x`. Reusing the d512 learning-rate pair at d768 reduced effective speedup to `0.894x`. Stop without Gate 2 or production upstreaming.

## Experiment

The canonical July baseline is #6882 at commit `52d8a9eb8d9434cf1dcaaee060edeadc60dfff9d`. Each attention and MoE merge in layer $l$ was changed to $\sqrt{1-\beta_l/L}\,r + \sqrt{\beta_l/L}\,h$, with $\beta_l=\operatorname{softplus}(\theta_l)$ and $\theta_l=0$ at initialization. One scalar $\theta_l$ was shared by both merges in each layer. Effective $\beta_l$ was capped just below $L$ to preserve the square-root domain.

Original request:

> Try to find the july baseline and try the following norm preserving residual
>
> `(sqrt(1 - beta_l / L)) residual + sqrt(beta_l / L) hidden`
>
> Here L is the total number of layer
> Parameterized beta to be a positive thing, perhaps `softplus(theta)` where `theta = 0`

## Results

| Run | Paloma macro | Final-100 tokens/s | Effective speedup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| July d512 baseline | 3.56670 | 352,609 | 1.000x |
| `MOE-NPR-001-d512` | 3.55702 | 340,730 | 1.018x |
| July d768 baseline | 3.22720 | 249,954 | 1.000x |
| `MOE-NPR-002-d768` | 3.22823 | 239,031 | 0.950x |
| `MOE-NPR-003-d768-d512lr` | 3.23768 | 239,305 | 0.894x |

All three W&B runs finished at their configured step counts. Iris reported exit 0 and zero failures. Final checkpoint metadata exists for every run. Mean learned beta moved from `0.6931` to `2.3024` at d512 and `2.6869` at d768, so the negative d768 result is not caused by a frozen gate.

The d512-LR transfer changed only the d768 LR pair: MuonH/AdamH LR `0.0083729565 -> 0.0098041002` and Adam LR `0.0019322207 -> 0.0022624847`. It worsened d768 Paloma macro loss by `0.00945` with a `0.11%` throughput gain.

## Links

- [Final snapshot](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/96b2fcb4eae6d5ff22668e2d2fcee0b3ebdb7c12)
- [Logbook](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/96b2fcb4eae6d5ff22668e2d2fcee0b3ebdb7c12/.agents/logbooks/norm-preserving-residual.md)
- [d512 W&B](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/dial_moe/runs/MOE-NPR-001-d512)
- [d768 W&B](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/dial_moe/runs/MOE-NPR-002-d768)
- [d768 d512-LR W&B](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/dial_moe/runs/MOE-NPR-003-d768-d512lr)

## Decision Log

- 2026-09-02: share one learned scalar across the attention and MoE residual merges in each transformer layer.
- 2026-09-02: require effective speedup above `1.0x` at both d512 and d768 before Gate 2.
- 2026-09-07: stop after Gate 1 because d768 reached `0.950x`.
- 2026-09-07: reject d512-LR transfer at d768 because it reached `0.894x`.

## Negative Results Index

- Norm-preserving residual mixing did not transfer its narrow d512 win to d768.
- The d512 learning-rate pair worsened d768 quality at nearly unchanged throughput.

## Conclusion

Do not run d1024/d1280 Gate 2 and do not upstream this residual formulation. These are single-seed results, so the `1.018x` d512 result may be noise; the required two-width criterion already rejects the series.

## Next Steps

No further work in this issue. Test a materially different residual parameterization or initialization in a new experiment issue.

issues.body:
## TL;DR

The archived Qwen3 optimizer harness is available in the closed, unmerged PR #7118. Error-aware Muon was evaluated at 130M and 300M with matched learning-rate controls. At 300M, the stabilized Hesscorr implementation completed all 15 gain/LR cells. Gains `0.1` and `0.3` each beat paired Muon at all five learning rates, but every Hesscorr variant lost to the simpler blend `0.05` baseline at all five learning rates and required about 90% more native training time than Muon.

The best 300M Hesscorr cell used gain `0.3`, learning rate `0.012`, and reached `1.057701` held-out Paloma C4-en BPB. Paired Muon reached `1.058626` (`-0.000925` for Hesscorr), while blend `0.05` reached `1.056606` (`+0.001095` for Hesscorr). This single-seed result establishes numerical stability and a small improvement over plain Muon, but not a favorable quality-per-compute tradeoff.

Exact stabilized source and materialized results: [`fffd6a64`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/fffd6a64ce81722f44d02d754db7c4778e0a5be5).

## Stabilized implementation

The original 300M Hesscorr sweep failed all 15 cells at global step 0. A warmup retry remained finite through step 50 and failed on step 51, the first corrected update, localizing the failure to the Sylvester correction.

The published implementation:

- uses ordinary quintic Muon for the first 50 optimizer updates, one momentum time constant at momentum `0.98`;
- uses explicit highest precision for polar-Hessian, Sylvester, and inverse matrix products;
- constructs the polar Hessian from one product and its transpose for exact post-rounding symmetry;
- computes the correction norm with scale-safe Frobenius normalization and falls back to a zero correction if the solve or norm is non-finite.

The [optimizer](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/fffd6a64ce81722f44d02d754db7c4778e0a5be5/experiments/speedrun/prism_berkeley_qwen3_scaling/muon_error_feedback_optimizer.py), [100-step TPU gate](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/fffd6a64ce81722f44d02d754db7c4778e0a5be5/experiments/speedrun/prism_berkeley_qwen3_scaling/muon_error_feedback_stability_gate.py), [15-cell launcher](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/fffd6a64ce81722f44d02d754db7c4778e0a5be5/experiments/speedrun/prism_berkeley_qwen3_scaling/muon_error_feedback_sweep.py), and [result materializer](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/fffd6a64ce81722f44d02d754db7c4778e0a5be5/experiments/speedrun/prism_berkeley_qwen3_scaling/materialize_muon_error_feedback_results.py) are pinned to the result commit.

## 300M held-out C4-en results

Lower BPB is better. Muon and blend `0.05` are completed same-geometry references from version `2026.07.23.4`; stabilized Hesscorr uses version `2026.08.28.3`.

| Variant | LR 0.004 | LR 0.006 | LR 0.008 | LR 0.010 | LR 0.012 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Muon | 1.067245 | 1.062251 | 1.060028 | 1.059351 | 1.058626 |
| Blend 0.05 | 1.066771 | 1.061070 | 1.059204 | 1.057656 | **1.056606** |
| Hesscorr 0.1 | 1.066853 | 1.062055 | 1.059515 | 1.058882 | 1.057950 |
| Hesscorr 0.3 | 1.067066 | 1.061869 | 1.059530 | 1.058388 | **1.057701** |
| Hesscorr 1.0 | 1.067755 | 1.062778 | 1.060028 | 1.058927 | 1.058036 |

| Hesscorr gain | Mean delta vs Muon | Wins vs Muon | Mean delta vs Blend 0.05 | Wins vs Blend | Mean time overhead vs Muon |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0.1 | -0.000449 | 5/5 | +0.000790 | 0/5 | +90.03% |
| 0.3 | -0.000589 | 5/5 | +0.000649 | 0/5 | +90.05% |
| 1.0 | +0.000005 | 2/5 | +0.001244 | 0/5 | +90.05% |

All 15 Hesscorr runs reached `global_step=11443`, wrote final checkpoint metadata, and had finite final loss. Iris reported zero failed cells and 124 aggregate preemptions. Each run processed 5,999,951,872 tokens on one preemptible v5p-8 slice in `us-central1`.

## 130M context

The earlier 40-cell 130M sweep found Hesscorr gain `0.1` improved C4-en BPB at four of five paired learning rates. Its best cell reached `1.164666` at learning rate `0.020`, versus `1.165484` for paired Muon, with a mean paired delta of `-0.000587` and 4.33% mean training-time overhead. The stabilized 300M result preserves the improvement over Muon but makes the compute tradeoff substantially worse.

## Artifacts and conclusion

- [Technical report with the full per-LR analysis](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/fffd6a64ce81722f44d02d754db7c4778e0a5be5/docs/reports/error-aware-muon-speedrun.md)
- [Machine-readable 130M and 300M results](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/fffd6a64ce81722f44d02d754db7c4778e0a5be5/experiments/speedrun/prism_berkeley_qwen3_scaling/muon_error_feedback_results.json)
- [300M debugging record](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/fffd6a64ce81722f44d02d754db7c4778e0a5be5/docs/debug-log-error-aware-muon-300m.md)
- [Best 300M Hesscorr W&B run](https://wandb.ai/understanding-sam/marin/runs/qwen3_300m_error_aware_muon_hesscorr-g0p3_lr0p012-2026.08.28.3)

The stabilization solves the numerical failure, but this implementation should not be scaled further by default: blend `0.05` is better at every paired learning rate and is roughly twice as fast. A future Hesscorr experiment should first reduce the Sylvester cost, then compare Hesscorr `0.3`, Muon, and blend `0.05` across multiple seeds at learning rates `0.010` and `0.012`.

A separate v4-8 copy in `us-central2` failed before W&B initialization because its workers rejected the `us-central1` FineWeb cache. It was not retried and is not evidence about optimizer quality or stability.

## Summary

This closed SFT experiment took the second Snowball 67B A2B cooldown checkpoint at native step 105149 through a reproducible cold-start post-training pipeline: Chat, then Thinking, then two protocol-matched Stage 3 branches for OpenCode and Nemotron Terminal. The workflow deliverable succeeded: the base and all completed stages were retained, exported, and evaluated with durable artifacts. The strongest conclusion is nuanced rather than uniformly positive. The three SFT stages cost about `1.232e20` training FLOPs and roughly 207 training-loop H100 GPU-hours, far less than the estimated extra pretraining compute from 2T to 5.7T tokens, and they produce large gains on AIME24, MATH500, and GSM8K 0-shot versus the 5.7T base. They also regress some competencies: across 51 sequential non-agentic score comparisons, 30 improve and 21 regress, and the issue does not support the stronger claim that every stage improves every benchmark. The valid agentic addendum shows the 5.7T Nemotron-Terminal branch passing infrastructure quality with 0.204 scoreable mean reward, while OpenCode remains very weak and the 2T Nemotron-Terminal reproduction misses the infrastructure-success gate.

- Full public analysis report: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/benjaminfeuer/standing-up-a-cold-start-sft-pipeline-for-marin-models/2026.08.16/index.html
- SFT launcher PR: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8172

<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Human Authored tl;dr

WHAT THIS IS: In this experiment, we take the 5.7T token cooldown of Marin 67B A2B "Snowball", run our current cold-start SFT pipeline on it, and eval every intermediate stage as well as the final stage on the standard benchmark cohort. We also report the canonical eval scores for the corresponding models on the 2T token cooldown (which were not reported previously as a single unit).
WHY WE DID IT: Provide a clear workflow for running our cold-start SFT on a cooled-down Marin checkpoint (a future blueprint to build on), and start to get a sense of where additional pretraining is impactful and where post-training has disproportionate impact.
RESULT: All stages of the SFT reproduction were successful, as was independent measurement. The clear workflow deliverable was achieved. For the benchmarks which regressed, further debugging / error decomposition will be needed to distinguish eval failures from pipeline failures.

comments.body:
🤖 Updated public record for issue 8225

## TL;DR

The second Snowball cooldown, taken after 5.7T pretraining tokens, passed through Chat and Thinking SFT, followed by separate OpenCode and Nemotron-Terminal Stage 3 branches. Snowball is a 67B-parameter mixture-of-experts model with about 2B active non-embedding parameters per token (67B A2B). The base model and every completed stage are public on Hugging Face. The three-stage Chat → Thinking → Nemotron-Terminal path improved AIME24, MATH500, and GSM8K 0-shot over the 5.7T base, but some benchmarks regressed. Across three transitions on 17 non-agentic benchmarks, 30 of 51 scores improved and 21 regressed.

## Setup

The starting checkpoint is [Snowball's second cooldown at step 105149](https://huggingface.co/laion/snowball-67b-a2b-cooldown-step105149/tree/b4d2656de8c39b699f7bbcbc878ca96996b319f3). It is the pre-SFT checkpoint used by the August fixed-EOT and Nemotron-Terminal experiments discussed in [#7743](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7743#issuecomment-5256454456). The [SFT launcher](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8172) and [data restoration](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8171) record the training recipes.

The stages form one dependency chain through Thinking, followed by two independent Stage 3 branches:

1. **Chat:** one packed epoch of [`nyu-dice-lab/wildchat50m-rewild-sft-385700` at revision `46a5bb5`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/nyu-dice-lab/wildchat50m-rewild-sft-385700/tree/46a5bb5).
2. **Thinking:** one packed epoch of [`laion/llama-nemotron-science-reasoning-on-canonical-think-full` at revision `bae881d`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/laion/llama-nemotron-science-reasoning-on-canonical-think-full/tree/bae881d), initialized from the final Chat checkpoint.
3. **OpenCode:** five token epochs over the fixed-EOT rendering of the [29-component OpenCode SFT mixture](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/grug-67b-a2b-agentic-sft-training-data/tree/a9805934c9c98908c611236bbfc87799f1ff6fe5/converted_hf), initialized from the final Thinking checkpoint. Fixed-EOT means that supervised assistant turns end with the tokenizer's end-of-turn token. The same release includes the [earlier per-component Levanter token caches](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/grug-67b-a2b-agentic-sft-training-data/tree/a9805934c9c98908c611236bbfc87799f1ff6fe5/token_caches), source manifest, chat template, row counts, and token counts. Those caches document the original 1,903-step lineage and are not the corrected consolidated cache used by this 1,888-step run. This checkpoint is evaluated with OpenCode on [`DCAgent/dev_set_v2` at `377118ff`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/DCAgent/dev_set_v2/tree/377118ff3031c934f5a647ae2c425eb74eef3b21).
4. **Nemotron Terminal:** 1,888 steps over the selected [`nvidia/Nemotron-Terminal-Corpus` files at revision `a1667c4`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/Nemotron-Terminal-Corpus/tree/a1667c4ffdadea02a89bffe4f1bb7ca2ff19f8d9/dataset_adapters), initialized independently from the same Thinking checkpoint. This is the #7743 control recipe and is evaluated with Terminus-2 on OpenThoughts-TBLite.

Each stage uses weights-only initialization with a fresh optimizer and step counter. Every final checkpoint is published in Hugging Face BF16 format.

## Goal

The ordered Chat → Thinking curriculum establishes the common prefix. The two Stage 3 branches test matching tool-use protocols: OpenCode trajectories with the OpenCode harness, and Nemotron-Terminal trajectories with Terminus-2.

## Status

The Base, Chat, Thinking, OpenCode, and Nemotron-Terminal checkpoints completed. The 5.7T and earlier 2T comparison cohorts have complete 17/17 non-agentic benchmark coverage. For this comparison, each cohort contains Base, Chat, Thinking, and Nemotron-Terminal checkpoints; OpenCode is evaluated separately with its matching agent harness. NQ-Open, TriviaQA, DROP, and OlympiadBench were rerun with one protocol across those eight checkpoints. The [revision-pinned public evaluation archive](https://huggingface.co/datasets/penfever/snowball-5.7t-sft-eval-artifacts/tree/a24bbff70bdbcfeeec5e1fb57fe12656b2bfb4f3) contains the result-selection manifest, raw records, configurations, and reported score tables.

The OpenCode and Nemotron-Terminal Stage 3 branches were evaluated with their matching OpenCode and Terminus-2 harnesses. Earlier cohorts used a mismatched agent protocol or failed before producing valid model outputs. They remain in the evaluation archive as negative controls and are excluded from the agentic-results table.

## Training accounting

All four SFT runs use 64 H100s, a global batch of 64 sequences, and a sequence length of 32,768 tokens. FLOPs use Levanter's analytic model with Snowball's routed top-4 experts, always-on shared expert, sliding-window attention, and long attention every fourth layer plus the final layer. The estimate is `7.05675264e9` forward FLOPs per token and `2.117025792e10` training FLOPs per token, including the language-model head. Stage FLOPs are `training FLOPs/token × steps × batch × sequence length`.

GPU-hours measure the training loop at the observed steady-state step rate. They exclude compilation, checkpoint serialization, retries, export, and evaluation. The OpenCode job consumed about 450 allocated GPU-hours over seven hours including checkpoint barriers, compared with about 141 GPU-hours spent advancing training steps.

| Stage | Steps | Packed tokens | Training FLOPs | Step rate | Training-loop GPU-hours | W&B | Observed loss |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- | --- |
| Chat | 257 | 0.539B | `1.14e19` | 3.92 s | ~18 | [run](https://wandb.ai/nyu-dice-lab/marin_moe_sft/runs/snowball_step105149_sft_s1_chat) | 0.648 at step 256 |
| Thinking | 630 | 1.321B | `2.80e19` | 3.7 s | ~41 | [run](https://wandb.ai/nyu-dice-lab/marin_moe_sft/runs/snowball_step105149_sft_s2_thinking) | 1.09 at step 39 → 0.998 at step 630 |
| OpenCode | 1,888 | 3.959B | `8.38e19` | 4.2 s | ~141 | tracker disabled | 0.497 at step 2 → 0.201 at step 1,888 |
| Nemotron Terminal | 1,888 | 3.959B | `8.38e19` | 4.4 s | ~148 | tracker disabled | 0.634 at step 44 → 0.484 near step 1,550; finite through completion |

The [Chat and Thinking loss curves](https://huggingface.co/datasets/penfever/snowball-5.7t-sft-eval-artifacts/blob/a24bbff70bdbcfeeec5e1fb57fe12656b2bfb4f3/training/sft_loss_curves.svg) come from the W&B runs. The Stage 3 launchers inherited the August recipe's disabled tracker, so their summaries come from retained progress logs. The sampled losses were finite and stable or decreasing through completion.

## Agentic results

These scores use the matching harness for each Stage 3 lineage. Each task verifier returns reward in `[0, 1]`; full reward is `1`. Trials with retained verifier rewards are scoreable even when the agent reached its time limit. Infrastructure failures without verifier rewards are excluded from the scoreable-trial mean and included as zero in the all-attempt mean. Harness and policy differences confound direct comparison between the OpenCode and Terminus-2 rows.

| Checkpoint | Policy and harness | Scoreable | Mean reward, scoreable | Mean reward, all 300 attempts | Full reward | Infrastructure gate |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| 5.7T OpenCode, step 1,888 | `DCAgent/dev_set_v2`, OpenCode | 291/300 (97.00%) | 0.01299 | 0.01260 | 3/300 | Pass |
| 5.7T Nemotron Terminal, step 1,888 | OpenThoughts-TBLite `dev_set_v2`, Terminus-2 | 293/300 (97.67%) | 0.20418 | 0.19942 | 56/300 | Pass |
| 2T Nemotron Terminal reproduction, step 1,888 | OpenThoughts-TBLite `dev_set_v2`, Terminus-2 | 259/300 (86.33%) | 0.16784 | 0.14490 | 39/300 | Fail |

The infrastructure gate requires at least 90% scoreable attempts. The [agentic addendum](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8225#issuecomment-5308091643) records failure counts and scoring rules. The revision-pinned [5.7T configurations](https://gist.github.com/penfever/34e22b004327aa220ccdcfc87b29a0ec/cfeaa1ad862586676f4de189cc2e8bcf067ea2f5) and [OpenThoughts-TBLite policy](https://gist.github.com/penfever/b40a3100a6decfaba83814a97c895f4b/ad4a2244dac7140923cddcfbf5a8a7075f0320fc) define the recorded harness settings. The executable OpenCode and Terminus-2 source revisions were not retained, so these records do not fully pin the harness implementations. The common Thinking parent was not evaluated under both matching agent harnesses; the endpoint scores do not establish a causal Stage 3 improvement.

## Downstream results

The following values are the selected rows in the public [evaluation score table](https://huggingface.co/datasets/penfever/snowball-5.7t-sft-eval-artifacts/blob/a24bbff70bdbcfeeec5e1fb57fe12656b2bfb4f3/eval-results/qa/EVAL_RESULTS.pdf). The archive's source-record manifest resolves each selected row to its raw evaluation record and excludes incomplete, protocol-mismatched, and superseded runs. Scores are percentages.

| Checkpoint | AIME24 | MATH500 | OlympiadBench | GSM8K 0-shot | DROP |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Base cooldown, step 105149 | 8.33 | 56.40 | 10.33 | 65.13 | 0.50 |
| Chat, step 257 | 14.00 | 75.60 | 20.33 | 82.41 | 67.08 |
| Thinking, step 630 | 23.00 | 70.00 | 13.67 | 89.01 | 35.21 |
| Nemotron Terminal, step 1,888 | 37.00 | 78.20 | 9.00 | 85.75 | 41.72 |

Chat produces the largest OlympiadBench result. Thinking and Nemotron Terminal improve AIME24 further, and Nemotron Terminal produces the largest MATH500 result. AIME24 and OlympiadBench each contain 30 distinct benchmark items here, so item-sampling uncertainty remains high. OlympiadBench uses ten generations per item, but those repeats do not increase the number of distinct items.

NQ-Open and TriviaQA were rerun for all eight 5.7T and 2T checkpoints with [Evalchemy at `cc98f653`](https://github.com/mlfoundations/evalchemy/commit/cc98f653), NQ-Open task v4.3, TriviaQA task v3.3, five shots, and a 128-token generation cap. The cap makes the results internally consistent but disadvantages the thinking models because reasoning tokens consume the same budget as the final answer.

| Checkpoint | NQ-Open | TriviaQA |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 5.7T Base | 33.05 | 75.95 |
| 5.7T Chat | 21.63 | 67.57 |
| 5.7T Thinking | 0.00 | 0.38 |
| 5.7T Nemotron Terminal | 1.16 | 12.89 |
| 2T Base | 29.56 | 72.02 |
| 2T Chat | 20.47 | 66.47 |
| 2T Thinking | 0.00 | 0.01 |
| 2T Nemotron Terminal | 1.05 | 15.92 |

DROP and OlympiadBench were rerun for all eight checkpoints with [Evalchemy at `5ec15cc`](https://github.com/mlfoundations/evalchemy/commit/5ec15cc). DROP uses three shots, a 256-token generation cap, and all 9,536 examples. OlympiadBench uses zero shots, the registered 32,768-token cap, and ten repeats of the 30-example subset; its evaluator reserves prompt headroom and uses a 31,680-token generation budget.

## Public artifacts

- [Base model, step 105149](https://huggingface.co/laion/snowball-67b-a2b-cooldown-step105149/tree/b4d2656de8c39b699f7bbcbc878ca96996b319f3)

- [Nemotron-Terminal SFT dataset](https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/Nemotron-Terminal-Corpus/tree/a1667c4ffdadea02a89bffe4f1bb7ca2ff19f8d9/dataset_adapters)

- [Final report, score table, loss data, and scaling audit](https://gist.github.com/penfever/0150d979810cb9fc3bad1cb92e2ab9c5)

- [Evaluation harvesting and audit tools](https://gist.github.com/penfever/0b98edb8be63faf8742f976c5f629c74)
- [Canonical OpenThoughts-TBLite configuration](https://gist.github.com/penfever/b40a3100a6decfaba83814a97c895f4b)
- [Matched DROP and OlympiadBench protocol](https://gist.github.com/penfever/23abc70648e597cfa947960675d2f98e)
- [Matched NQ-Open and TriviaQA protocol](https://gist.github.com/penfever/a8b39acaa4a684867b723f6993e59622)
- [Configurations used to fill missing benchmark cells](https://gist.github.com/penfever/777025360c5204c79d9ad4289ac91cbf)
- [Stage evaluation and agentic harness configurations](https://gist.github.com/penfever/34e22b004327aa220ccdcfc87b29a0ec)
- [Earlier 2T comparison configurations](https://gist.github.com/penfever/6b35ebbdbaf93c2982c44d66f59d348f)

The public 2T comparison checkpoints are [Chat](https://huggingface.co/penfever/grug-67b-a2b-sft-s1-wildchat-step257/tree/16989a23624f7a839b937aa21204873bd54bff65), [Thinking](https://huggingface.co/penfever/grug-67b-a2b-sft-s2-thinking-step630/tree/b1941773d0a1469ba3c316853aa5f3f8c2b9d715), and [Nemotron-Terminal](https://huggingface.co/laion/sft-repro-thinking-step630-nemotron-terminal-step1888/tree/0ef753164bb3004f23b5dca904f27e40710ce48e). The evaluated 2T base checkpoint is not publicly released; the score table and raw evaluation records remain public.

## Decision log

- 2026-08-13: Use the second cooldown at step 105149, matching the August fixed-EOT and Nemotron-Terminal starting checkpoint.
- 2026-08-13: Preserve a strict dependency chain. Agentic does not initialize directly from the cooldown checkpoint in this campaign.
- 2026-08-13: Use the restored source in #8171 and #8172; keep campaign-specific source changes in #8172.

## Conclusion

The ordered pipeline completed. Across the 51 sequential non-agentic score comparisons, 30 improve and 21 regress. Chat improves 13/17 benchmarks over the 5.7T base, Thinking improves 5/17 over Chat, and Nemotron Terminal improves 12/17 over Thinking. The final Nemotron-Terminal checkpoint gains 28.67 points on AIME24, 21.80 on MATH500, and 20.62 on GSM8K 0-shot relative to the 5.7T base, while losing 1.33 points on OlympiadBench.

The Chat → Thinking → Nemotron-Terminal path consumes an estimated `1.232e20` training FLOPs and approximately 207 training-loop H100 GPU-hours. This sum excludes the alternative OpenCode branch. Extending pretraining from 2T to 5.7T tokens costs an estimated `7.83e22` FLOPs under the same analytic model, approximately 636 times the three-stage SFT compute. This is a compute comparison, not a claim that the two interventions produce equivalent capabilities. The experiment does not show that every substage improves every competency without regression.

spillover_issues.body:
`CloudGcpService` uses two GCP clients: a REST `httpx.Client` for the v2 TPU/compute/logging surfaces, and a gRPC `tpu_v2alpha1.TpuClient` used *only* for the four queued-resource (reserved-TPU) methods — `create/get/delete/list_queued_resources` (`lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/gcp/service.py`).

Consider porting those four methods onto the REST client so the class has a single transport, a single auth mechanism, and uniform error handling. That would also let us delete the lazy-init + lock around `_tpu_alpha_client` and drop the `google-cloud-tpu` dependency.

Trade-offs the implementer should weigh:
- Queued resources currently live on the `v2alpha1` surface, while the REST helpers target stable `v2`. Check whether queued resources are reachable on `v2` (GA) before committing — if so this is low-risk and reuses `_paginate` / `tpu_operation_status` directly; if not, a REST port means hand-built JSON on an alpha surface (field-churn risk) plus LRO wiring.
- The gRPC client currently provides typed request/response protos and pagination for free; REST would hand-assemble/parse those.
- The lazy gRPC client constructor resolves ADC eagerly, so any port must preserve the class's "construct cheaply, authenticate on first call" contract.

Not urgent — the lazy-init race was already fixed in #6435. This is a consistency/dependency cleanup; implementer decides scope and whether it's worth doing now.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:**
- [x] Actionability check — actionable (named file/methods, clear definition of done)
- [x] Duplicate-work preflight (no overlapping PR; #6435 already landed the lazy-init fix)
- [x] Resolve the central risk: are queued resources on GA `v2` REST?
- [x] Scope the port + post analysis
- [ ] Human decision on whether to implement now (scope left to implementer per issue)

# Research

The blocking question — *"Check whether queued resources are reachable on `v2` (GA) before committing"* — resolves **yes**. This is the low-risk branch the issue describes: the REST port reuses `_paginate` / `_classify_response` / `tpu_operation_status` directly, with no hand-built JSON on an alpha surface.

Evidence:
- Installed GA `google.cloud.tpu_v2` exposes the full queued-resource proto set: `CreateQueuedResourceRequest`, `GetQueuedResourceRequest`, `DeleteQueuedResourceRequest`, `ListQueuedResourcesRequest`, `QueuedResource`, `QueuedResourceState` (alpha only adds `PerformMaintenance…`).
- The `v2` REST reference page `projects.locations.queuedResources` exists (301-redirects, not 404).

**Relevant code**
- [`service.py#L669-L777`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/gcp/service.py#L669-L777) — the 4 gRPC methods + `_qr_api_error`
- [`service.py#L419-L425`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/gcp/service.py#L419-L425) — lazy `_tpu_alpha_client` to delete
- [`service.py#L535-L557`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/gcp/service.py#L535-L557) — `tpu_operation_status`, reusable for the create LRO
- [`pyproject.toml#L24`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/pyproject.toml#L24) — `google-cloud-tpu>=1.18.0` to drop
- [`test_gcp_service.py#L362-L395`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/tests/cluster/backends/gcp/test_gcp_service.py#L362-L395) — two MagicMock queued-resource tests

# Proposed approach

Port all four methods onto the REST `httpx.Client` at `{_TPU_BASE}/{parent}/queuedResources`, then delete the gRPC client, `_qr_api_error`, the `tpu_v2alpha1` / `google.api_core` imports, and the `google-cloud-tpu` dep.

- **create** — `POST …/queuedResources?queuedResourceId={name}` with body `{"tpu":{"nodeSpec":[{"parent":…,"nodeId":name,"node":{…}}]},"guaranteed":{"reserved":true}}`; classify via `_classify_response`. Matches current gRPC behavior, which fires the create and ignores the returned LRO. (Design note: if we later want fail-fast on queued-resource create like `tpu_create`, capture the op name and poll `tpu_operation_status` — out of scope unless wanted.)
- **describe** — `GET …/queuedResources/{name}`; `state = data["state"]["state"]` (default `"UNKNOWN"`); 404→None.
- **delete** — `DELETE …/queuedResources/{name}?force=true`; swallow 404.
- **list** — `_paginate(parent/queuedResources, "queuedResources")`; labels live at `tpu.nodeSpec[0].node.labels`; keep the wildcard-zone extraction from the resource name.
- **tests** — convert the two MagicMock tests to the existing `httpx.MockTransport` fake (consistent with the rest of the file); add create/describe/delete coverage asserting URL/params and 404→None.

Estimated ~120–180 lines incl. tests; net deletion of a transport, a dependency, and the lazy-client lock. `fake.py` (InMemory) is unaffected.

The issue says *"implementer decides scope and whether it's worth doing now."* The risk is now resolved and the change is mechanical, but it removes a dependency and migrates an API surface, so I'm flagging for a human go-ahead before opening a PR. Reply here to greenlight and I'll implement.

spillover_issues.body:
## Description
Rewrite implementation-pinned tests so they check public behavior instead of private representation, helper dispatch, or call counts.

Primary examples: lib/haliax/tests/test_named_ref.py, tests/execution/test_artifact_registry.py, tests/rl/test_replay_buffer.py, lib/levanter/tests/test_tokenizers.py, lib/haliax/tests/test_ragged_dot_dispatch.py, and lib/levanter/tests/kernels/test_pallas_fused_cross_entropy_loss.py.

### Definition of Done
- Private _prefix/_root/_is_rollout_fresh assertions are replaced by public behavior checks or a named public inspection API.
- Mock call-count assertions are secondary to observable files, results, warnings, or fake boundary state.
- Refactors that preserve behavior are less likely to break these tests.

Parent audit: #6424

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:**
- [x] Read the 6 implementation-pinned test files + the code they test
- [x] Scope decision: multi-module (haliax/levanter/marin), spans 6 files, includes a design question → **analysis-only, no PR** per the larger-than-bugfix rule
- [x] Post Research + per-file proposed rewrites for human review

# Research

Per parent audit #6424 finding #3 (S3) and #5 (S3/S8): these tests assert private representation (`_prefix`/`_ref`/`_root`), call directly into private helpers (`_is_rollout_fresh`), or assert mock call counts (`assert_not_called`/`assert_called_once`) as the *primary* signal. They break under behavior-preserving refactors and miss externally visible regressions.

Not opening a PR: this touches three modules and the cleanest fix for `NamedRef` raises a design question (is the composed-index encoding part of the contract, or test-only?) that the maintainer should decide first. Proposing per-file rewrites below; once an approach is picked I can split into per-module PRs.

**Relevant code**
- [`replay_buffer.py#L124`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/rl/replay_buffer.py#L124) — `_is_rollout_fresh`; already observable via `add_batches`/`set_current_step`/`size`
- [`ref.py#L372-L379`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/haliax/src/haliax/ref.py#L372) — `slice()` builds `_prefix`; writes through it are the real contract
- [`test_tokenizers.py#L1474-L1542`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/tests/test_tokenizers.py#L1474) — staging dispatch asserted via mock call counts

# Proposed approach (per file)

**1. `tests/rl/test_replay_buffer.py:445` `test_is_rollout_fresh` — highest value, self-contained.**
Delete the private-method test. `create_test_batch` already accepts `weight_step=` and `timestamp=`, and the file at L403-442 already proves freshness through `add_batches` + `set_current_step(...)` + `size()`. Rewrite the four cases (step-window min, future weight_step, stale timestamp) as add-batches-then-assert-`size()`/`sample_rollouts()`. No private access; fails on real filtering regressions.

**2. `lib/levanter/tests/test_tokenizers.py:1474-1542` staging dispatch — replace call-count asserts with file provenance.**
Make each fake source write *distinguishable* bytes (mirror→`"MIRROR"`, hf→`"HF"`). Then assert the staged `tokenizer.json` *content* instead of `mock.assert_not_called()`:
- cache-hit: pre-seed cache, assert staged bytes are the cached ones (hf/mirror fakes that would write different bytes leave it unchanged);
- mirror-hit: staged bytes == mirror's;
- corrupt-mirror: mirror writes `"not json"`, assert final staged file is the valid hf copy.
Call counts may stay as a *secondary* assertion. Separately, the type-only tests at L356-420 (`isinstance(MarinTokenizer)`, `all_special_ids is list`, `encode_returns_list_of_ints`) are S2 tautologies already covered by the roundtrip tests at L438 — collapse them (keep the special-token-id constants; those are a real contract).

**3. `lib/haliax/tests/test_named_ref.py` — behavior vs public inspection API (design question).**
`test_dslice_combination_branches` (L85-148) and the `_prefix`/`_ref` asserts (L82, L169-170, L221) pin the internal slice encoding. The real contract is *index composition*: after `ds_ref.slice({...})`, writing a sentinel through the sub-ref should land in exactly the corresponding base-ref cells. Rewrite each branch as write-through-sub-ref → read base → assert affected/unaffected cells (covers dslice+slice, dslice+dslice, int, negative, list, array, strided composition without naming `dslice`). `unsliced._ref is base._ref` → assert a write through `unsliced` is visible in `base`. **Decision needed:** if the composed-index encoding is meant to be contract (e.g. for kernel authors), expose a public inspection API and assert that instead of `_prefix`.

**4. `lib/levanter/tests/kernels/test_pallas_fused_cross_entropy_loss.py:1107+` — low.**
`called["pallas"]==1`/`called["xla"]==1` already sit alongside a `pytest.warns(... "vmem compile OOM")` and the fallback path. Make the observable output primary (assert the returned loss equals the xla fake's result); keep counts secondary.

**5. `lib/haliax/tests/test_ragged_dot_dispatch.py` — low / partly no clean surface.**
`calls == [_DEFAULT_DIM_NUMS, _DLHS_DIM_NUMS, _DRHS_DIM_NUMS]` (L121) is redundant with the grad-correctness asserts above it (L118-120) — drop or soften it. `_triton_default_block_sizes` tests (L76-85) pin an internal heuristic with no public behavior; recommend leaving as explicit internal-heuristic guards or removing — there's no observable contract to convert them to.

**6. `tests/execution/test_artifact_registry.py` — low; file is mostly good already.**
`test_manifest_layout` (L137) reads `_root` but is really asserting the on-disk wire format, which *is* a cross-reader contract — keep (optionally via a small public path accessor). `test_root_normalizes_trailing_slash` (L156) and the `get_default_registry` `_root` checks (L261, L266) can instead assert via where a registered manifest lands (observable) rather than the private attr.

**Suggested batching:** (a) marin (`test_replay_buffer`, `test_artifact_registry`), (b) levanter (`test_tokenizers` staging, kernel fallback), (c) haliax (`test_named_ref`, `test_ragged_dot_dispatch`) — gated on the NamedRef decision. Items 1 and 2 are the highest leverage and lowest risk.

## Description
Replace runtime validation implemented with assert and narrow broad best-effort exception swallowing in Marin runtime paths.

Primary examples: lib/marin/src/marin/rl/environments/inference_ctx/render.py, lib/marin/src/marin/rl/rollout_worker.py, lib/marin/src/marin/rl/weight_transfer/arrow_flight.py, lib/marin/src/marin/transform/conversation/transform_conversation.py, lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evaluators/evalchemy_evaluator.py, and lib/marin/src/marin/execution/executor.py.

### Definition of Done
- Externally reachable validation raises explicit exceptions instead of assert.
- Intentional best-effort fallbacks catch expected exception types and log useful context.
- Tests cover the new validation/fallback behavior.

Parent audit: #6424

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Analysis — multi-module, no PR (per scope guidance).** This is a 6-file cleanup spanning four subsystems with a DoD requiring tests at each site, so it exceeds the self-contained single-PR bar. Recommend splitting into two focused PRs (below). Line numbers re-checked against current `main` (`81c92c6`) — three of the listed swallow sites are already narrowed and need no change.

# Research

Two distinct defects from audit #6424: `assert` used for externally-reachable validation (S7, vanishes under `python -O`), and broad `except Exception` with no logged context masking real failures (S6).

**S7 — assert as validation** ([render.py](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/rl/environments/inference_ctx/render.py))
- L202 `Llama3Renderer._render_message` — `assert message.get("thinking") is None`; reachable from any caller passing a `thinking` message.
- L277 `Qwen3Renderer._render_message` — same assert.
- L326 `Qwen3Renderer._end_message_token` — `assert len(tokens) == 1`; tokenizer-config invariant, reachable via a tokenizer lacking a single `<|im_end|>` token.

**S6 — broad swallows still open**
- [rollout_worker.py#L624](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/rl/rollout_worker.py#L624) — `except Exception: pass`, no log; transient run_state RPC failures are invisible.
- [arrow_flight.py#L93](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/rl/weight_transfer/arrow_flight.py#L93) — `except Exception: pass` around the GCP metadata fetch; should narrow to `urllib.error.URLError`/`OSError`/`socket.timeout` and log at debug.
- [executor.py#L321](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/execution/executor.py#L321) — `except Exception: return None` around `current_client()`; silently disables TPU region inference.

**Already narrowed on `main` — no action needed**
- [transform_conversation.py#L113](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/transform/conversation/transform_conversation.py#L113) — already `except json.JSONDecodeError` (keeps args raw). Only open question from the audit: tag-as-unparsed vs raw; raw is defensible, leave as-is unless product wants tagging.
- [evalchemy_evaluator.py#L96](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evaluators/evalchemy_evaluator.py#L96) (`_TeeWriter`) — already `except (OSError, ValueError)` with a teardown comment.
- [evalchemy_evaluator.py#L250](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evaluators/evalchemy_evaluator.py#L250) — outer already `logger.warning(...)`; only the nested `wandb.finish(exit_code=1)` swallow remains (acceptable teardown best-effort).

# Proposed Approach

**PR 1 (S7, testable, self-contained):** in `render.py` replace the three asserts with explicit exceptions carrying context — `NotImplementedError(f"CoT/thinking not supported in {type(self).__name__}")` for L202/L277, and `ValueError(f"Expected single token for <|im_end|>, got {len(tokens)}: {tokens}")` for L326. Tests: each renderer raises on a `thinking` message, and `_end_message_token` raises for a tokenizer that splits `<|im_end|>`.

**PR 2 (S6):** narrow + log the three open swallows. rollout_worker L624 → `except Exception: logger.debug("run_state check failed (best-effort)", exc_info=True)`; arrow_flight L93 → catch `(urllib.error.URLError, OSError, socket.timeout)` + debug log; executor L321 → debug log before `return None`. The fallback behavior is unchanged, so the only test worth adding is that the metadata-fetch helper falls back to hostname when the request raises; the rest is pure observability and warrants no test.

Holding here for a maintainer to confirm the split before implementing (esp. `NotImplementedError` vs `ValueError` for the CoT asserts, and whether transform_conversation should tag unparsed args).
